groups.title: BrightHome Appliances: Five-Year Sales and Revenue

stimulus.text:
BrightHome Appliances sells three products: X, Y and Z. The table below shows the number of units sold (in thousands) of each product from 2020 to 2024. The selling price per unit was constant throughout these years: ₹200 for X, ₹150 for Y and ₹300 for Z. (1 lakh = 1,00,000)

Year | X (thousand units) | Y (thousand units) | Z (thousand units)
2020 | 40 | 30 | 20
2021 | 50 | 36 | 25
2022 | 45 | 48 | 30
2023 | 60 | 54 | 24
2024 | 72 | 60 | 36

questions.text: In which year was the percentage growth in the total units sold (X + Y + Z) over the previous year the highest?
By how much (in ₹ lakh) did the total revenue from product X over the five years exceed the total revenue from product Y over the same period?
questions.explanation: Revenue of X per thousand units = 1,000 × ₹200 = ₹2 lakh. Revenue of Y per thousand units = 1,000 × ₹150 = ₹1.5 lakh. Total units of X = 40 + 50 + 45 + 60 + 72 = 267 thousand, so revenue = 267 × 2 = ₹534 lakh. Total units of Y = 30 + 36 + 48 + 54 + 60 = 228 thousand, so revenue = 228 × 1.5 = ₹342 lakh. Difference = 534 − 342 = ₹192 lakh.

questions.text: What percentage of the total revenue of the company in 2024 came from product X (approximately)?
questions.explanation: Revenue in 2024: X = 72 × 2 = ₹144 lakh. Y = 60 × 1.5 = ₹90 lakh. Z = 36 × 3 = ₹108 lakh (₹300 per unit gives ₹3 lakh per thousand units). Total = 144 + 90 + 108 = ₹342 lakh. Share of X = 144 / 342 × 100 ≈ 42.1%.

questions.text: If the price of product X had been increased by 10% in 2024 with no change in the units sold of any product, what would the total revenue of the company in 2024 have been (in ₹ lakh)?
questions.explanation: Original revenue of X in 2024 = ₹144 lakh. With a 10% price increase, revenue of X = 144 × 1.10 = ₹158.4 lakh. Revenue of Y = ₹90 lakh and revenue of Z = ₹108 lakh remain unchanged. New total = 158.4 + 90 + 108 = ₹356.4 lakh.

questions.text: What was the average revenue per unit sold of the company over the two years 2022 and 2023 taken together (approximately)?
questions.explanation: Revenue in 2022: X = 45 × 2 = 90. Y = 48 × 1.5 = 72. Z = 30 × 3 = 90. Total = ₹252 lakh. Revenue in 2023: X = 60 × 2 = 120. Y = 54 × 1.5 = 81. Z = 24 × 3 = 72. Total = ₹273 lakh. Combined revenue = 252 + 273 = ₹525 lakh = ₹5,25,00,000. Combined units = 123 + 138 = 261 thousand = 2,61,000 units. Average revenue per unit = 5,25,00,000 / 2,61,000 ≈ ₹201.15.

stimulus.text: Directions: Each of the questions below consists of a question and two statements numbered I and II given below it. You must decide whether the information provided in the statements is sufficient to answer the question. Consider the following while answering the questions: Mark 1 as the answer, if the question can be answered by using one of the statements alone but cannot be answered using the other statement alone. Mark 2 as the answer, if the question can be answered by using either statement alone. Mark 3 as the answer, if the question can be answered by using both statements together but cannot be answered using either statement alone. Mark 4 as the answer, if the question cannot be answered even by using both statements together.

options.1: One statement alone is sufficient, the other alone is not
options.4: Even both together are not sufficient

questions.text:
What is the two-digit number?
I. The sum of its digits is 9.
II. The number obtained by reversing its digits is 27 more than the original number.
questions.explanation: Let the number be 10a + b. From I alone, a + b = 9, which fits 18, 27, 36, 45 and others, so it is not sufficient. From II alone, (10b + a) − (10a + b) = 9(b − a) = 27, so b − a = 3, which fits 14, 25, 36, 47, 58 and 69, so it is not sufficient. Together, a + b = 9 and b − a = 3 give b = 6 and a = 3, so the number is 36. Both statements are needed, so the answer is 3.

questions.text:
Is the positive integer n a perfect square?
I. n has exactly 9 factors.
II. n is divisible by 4.
questions.explanation: From I, a number with exactly 9 factors is either p^8 or p^2 × q^2 for primes p and q. Both forms are perfect squares, so the answer is definitely yes. (Equivalently, only perfect squares have an odd number of factors.) From II, n = 4 is a perfect square but n = 8 is not, so no single answer is possible. Statement I alone is sufficient and II alone is not, so the answer is 1.

questions.text:
What is the average age of a group of 5 people?
I. The sum of the ages of the oldest and the youngest person is 60 years.
II. The ages of the five people are in arithmetic progression.
questions.explanation: From I alone, only the two extreme ages are known, so the other three ages can vary and the average cannot be fixed. From II alone, the ages are in arithmetic progression but no value is given, so the average cannot be found. Together, for an arithmetic progression of 5 terms, the average equals the middle term, which equals (first + last) / 2 = 60 / 2 = 30 years. Both statements are needed, so the answer is 3.

questions.text:
A and B together can complete a piece of work in 12 days. In how many days can A alone complete it?
I. B alone can complete the work in 30 days.
II. A is 1.5 times as efficient as B.
questions.explanation: From I, A's one-day work = 1/12 − 1/30 = 5/60 − 2/60 = 3/60 = 1/20, so A alone takes 20 days. From II, let B's one-day work be b, so A's is 1.5b. Then 2.5b = 1/12, so b = 1/30 and A's one-day work = 1.5/30 = 1/20, so A alone takes 20 days. Either statement alone is sufficient, so the answer is 2.

questions.text:
What is the area of triangle ABC?
I. AB = 6 cm and BC = 8 cm.
II. Triangle ABC is a right-angled triangle.
questions.explanation: From I alone, two sides are known but the angle between them is not, so the area cannot be found. From II alone, no side length is given. Together, the position of the right angle is still unknown. If the right angle is at B, the legs are 6 and 8 and the area is (1/2) × 6 × 8 = 24 sq cm. If the right angle is at A, then BC = 8 is the hypotenuse, AC = √(64 − 36) = √28, and the area is (1/2) × 6 × √28 = 3√28 ≈ 15.87 sq cm. Since different areas are possible, the question cannot be answered even with both statements. The answer is 4.

stimulus.text: Directions: In each question below, statements are given, followed by four conclusions numbered I, II, III and IV. Take the given statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts. Decide which of the conclusions logically follow from the statements, and select the option that gives the correct set of conclusions.

questions.text:
Statements: All forests are hills. Some hills are rivers. No river is a desert. All deserts are plains.
Conclusions:
I. Some hills are not deserts.
II. Some plains are not rivers.
III. Some forests are rivers.
IV. Some rivers are not plains.
options: Only I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: Some hills are rivers and no river is a desert, so those hills are not deserts. Hence I follows. All deserts are plains, so some plains are deserts, and no desert is a river, so those plains are not rivers. Hence II follows. III does not follow, because the hills that are rivers need not be forests. IV does not follow, because rivers are not linked definitely with plains, and some rivers may be plains. So only I and II follow.

questions.text:
Statements: No sheet is a page. Some pages are leaves.
Conclusions:
I. Some leaves are not sheets.
II. Some sheets are leaves.
III. No sheet is a leaf.
IV. Some pages are not sheets.
options: Only I, IV and either II or III follow
Only I, II and IV follow
questions.explanation: Some pages are leaves and no page is a sheet, so those leaves are not sheets. Hence I follows. No sheet is a page means no page is a sheet, and since some pages exist, some pages are not sheets. Hence IV follows. Conclusions II and III ('Some sheets are leaves' and 'No sheet is a leaf') form a complementary pair, because one of them must be true but neither is definite alone. So either II or III follows. The correct set is I, IV and either II or III.

questions.text:
Statements: All shirts are coats. No coat is a tie. Some ties are caps.
Conclusions:
I. No shirt is a tie.
II. Some caps are not coats.
III. Some caps are not shirts.
IV. Some coats are not caps.
options: Only I, II and III follow
All I, II, III and IV follow
questions.explanation: All shirts are coats and no coat is a tie, so no shirt is a tie. Hence I follows. Some ties are caps and no tie is a coat, so those caps are not coats. Hence II follows. Those caps are not coats, and every shirt is a coat, so they are not shirts either. Hence III follows. IV does not follow, because nothing definite links coats with caps. So only I, II and III follow.

questions.text:
Statements: Some kites are birds. All birds are planes. No plane is a boat.
Conclusions:
I. No kite is a boat.
II. Some kites are not boats.
III. It is possible that some kites are boats.
IV. All kites are planes.
questions.explanation: Some kites are birds and all birds are planes, so those kites are planes. No plane is a boat, so those kites are not boats. Hence II follows. Only some kites are known to be birds, so the remaining kites are not restricted, and it is possible that some of them are boats. Hence III follows. I does not follow, because the kites that are not birds may be boats. IV does not follow, because only some kites are birds. So only II and III follow.

questions.text:
Statements: Some cats are dogs. All dogs are rats. No rat is a bat. Some bats are owls.
Conclusions:
I. Some cats are not bats.
II. Some owls are not rats.
III. Some cats are owls.
IV. No dog is an owl.
options: Only I, II and III follow
Only II, III and IV follow
questions.explanation: Some cats are dogs and all dogs are rats, so those cats are rats. No rat is a bat, so those cats are not bats. Hence I follows. Some bats are owls and no bat is a rat, so those owls are not rats. Hence II follows. III does not follow, because nothing definitely links cats with owls. IV does not follow, because owls that are not bats may still be dogs. So only I and II follow.

stimulus.text: Seven guests (Arjun, Bela, Charu, Dinesh, Esha, Farhan and Gita) have been invited to a seminar. Whether each one attends depends on the following conditions: (i) If Arjun attends, then Bela does not attend. (ii) If Charu attends, then Arjun attends. (iii) If Dinesh does not attend, then Bela attends. (iv) If Esha attends, then Dinesh does not attend. (v) If Farhan attends, then Esha attends.

conditions: If Arjun attends, then Bela does not attend
If Charu attends, then Arjun attends
If Dinesh does not attend, then Bela attends
If Esha attends, then Dinesh does not attend
If Farhan attends, then Esha attends

questions.text: If Farhan attends, then which of the following must be true?
questions.explanation: By (v), Farhan attending means Esha attends. By (iv), Esha attending means Dinesh does not attend. By (iii), Dinesh not attending means Bela attends. By (i), Bela attending means Arjun does not attend (otherwise Bela would be absent). By (ii), Charu cannot attend, since her attendance would force Arjun's. So Bela attends, while Arjun, Charu and Dinesh do not. The answer is (b).

questions.text: If Charu attends, then which of the following must be true?
questions.explanation: By (ii), Charu attending means Arjun attends. By (i), Arjun attending means Bela does not attend. By (iii), if Dinesh did not attend then Bela would have to attend, so Dinesh must attend. By (iv), if Esha attended then Dinesh would not, so Esha does not attend. By (v), if Farhan attended then Esha would, so Farhan does not attend. So Dinesh must attend, while Bela, Esha and Farhan do not. The answer is (c).

questions.text: If Dinesh does not attend, then which of the following must NOT be true?
questions.explanation: By (iii), Dinesh not attending means Bela attends. By (i), Bela attending means Arjun does not attend. So 'Arjun attends' must be false. Esha and Farhan are not ruled out, because Esha attending only requires Dinesh to be absent, which holds, and Farhan attending only requires Esha to attend. Charu is also absent by (ii). So only option (a) must be false. The answer is (a).

questions.text: Which of the following could be the group of people attending the seminar?
questions.explanation: Option (a): Charu attends but Arjun does not, which violates (ii). Option (b): Charu attends and Arjun attends, satisfying (ii). Arjun attends and Bela is absent, satisfying (i). Dinesh attends, so (iii) holds. Esha and Farhan are absent, so (iv) and (v) hold. This group is valid. Option (c): Arjun and Bela both attend, which violates (i). Option (d): Esha and Dinesh both attend, which violates (iv). The answer is (b).

questions.text: What is the maximum number of guests who can attend the seminar?
questions.explanation: Case 1: Esha attends. Then Dinesh, Bela's partner chain gives Bela attending, and Arjun and Charu are absent. Farhan and Gita are free, so the largest group is Bela, Esha, Farhan and Gita, which is 4. Case 2: Esha does not attend. Then Farhan does not attend either, by (v). The remaining guests are Arjun, Bela, Charu, Dinesh and Gita. Arjun and Bela cannot both attend, so at most 4 can attend. Arjun, Charu, Dinesh and Gita is a valid group of 4. In no case can 5 attend, so the maximum is 4. The answer is (b).

groups.title: Critical Reasoning (Hard): Four-Day Work Week at Nexora Software

stimulus.text: Nexora Software, a company with 600 employees, plans to shift from a five-day work week to a four-day work week from April 1, with the working hours per day increased from 8 to 10 so that the weekly hours remain 40. The management argues that the change will raise employee productivity, since employees will have more rest and will therefore work with greater focus. In a six-month pilot involving 60 employees from the testing department, the number of software defects found per week rose by 15%, while the number of employees who reported feeling 'well rested' rose from 35% to 70%. The testing department's work is mostly routine and its output is measured in defects found.

metadata.claim: A four-day work week will raise productivity

questions.text: Which of the following statements, if true, most weakens the management's argument that the four-day week will raise productivity across the company?
options: Employees in the pilot said they enjoyed having a three-day weekend.

The testing department's work is routine and easy to measure, whereas most of the company's work, such as designing new software, requires sustained creative effort that suffers when workdays become longer and more tiring.
The company will save on office electricity costs on the fifth day.
The pilot lasted six months, which is longer than most company trials.
questions.explanation: The management generalises from the testing department to the whole company. Option (b) shows that the pilot department is unlike most of the company, and that longer days may harm the kind of work done elsewhere, so the generalisation is weakened. Option (a) supports the plan by showing that employees like it. Option (c) concerns costs, not productivity. Option (d) makes the pilot more reliable and so strengthens the management's case. The answer is (b).

questions.text: The management's argument that rest leads to higher productivity relies on which of the following assumptions?
options: The rise in defects found in the pilot was caused by employees feeling better rested, and not by some other factor.
All employees in the company work in the testing department.
The company will not hire any new employees after April 1.
Employees who feel well rested never take leave.
questions.explanation: The argument links the pilot result (more defects found) to better rest. This link works only if the rest, and not another factor such as a new testing tool or an easier batch of software, caused the rise. Option (a) states this assumption. Option (b) is false and unnecessary. Options (c) and (d) have no bearing on the link between rest and productivity. The answer is (a).

questions.text: Which of the following statements, if true, most strengthens the claim that better rest was the reason for the rise in defects found during the pilot?
options: The software tested during the pilot was more complex than the software tested in earlier months.
A similar group of 60 testers who stayed on the five-day week during the same six months showed no change in defects found.
Testers in the pilot were given new automated testing tools at the start of the six months.
The pilot testers were chosen because they were the most experienced in the department.
questions.explanation: A comparison group that stayed on the five-day week and showed no change rules out outside causes that would have affected all testers equally, such as seasonal workload or the nature of the software. This strengthens the claim that the new schedule and rest caused the rise. Option (a) does not help, since more complex software would be expected to lower, not raise, defects found, and in any case it adds a competing factor. Option (c) offers an alternative explanation and so weakens the claim. Option (d) suggests that selection, not rest, explains the result, which also weakens the claim. The answer is (b).

questions.text: Which of the following can be properly inferred from the passage?
options: The four-day week will raise productivity in every department of the company.
The pilot showed that employees who feel well rested find more defects than those who do not.
In the pilot, the share of employees who felt well rested doubled while defects found per week rose by 15%.
The weekly working hours of employees will fall under the new plan.
questions.explanation: The passage says that the 'well rested' share rose from 35% to 70%, which is a doubling, and that defects found rose by 15%. Option (c) restates these facts accurately. Option (a) goes beyond the evidence, since only one department was tested. Option (b) claims a cause that the passage does not establish. Option (d) is contradicted, because the weekly hours remain 40. The answer is (c).

questions.text: Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the management's claim that the plan will raise productivity company-wide?
options: Whether the output of other departments, such as software design, changes under longer working days.
The number of employees in the testing department who own a car.
The colour scheme of the company's new office.
The name of the manager who proposed the plan.
questions.explanation: The claim concerns the whole company, but the evidence comes only from the testing department. Knowing how output in other departments, especially those doing creative work, changes under 10-hour days directly tests whether the result generalises. Options (b), (c) and (d) are unrelated to productivity. The answer is (a).

groups.title: Sentence Completion (Hard): Grammar, Idiom and Double Blanks

stimulus.text: Directions: Each sentence below has one or two blanks. Choose the option that fits in grammatically and logically and completes the sentence most effectively. Some questions test grammar structures such as inverted conditionals, while others test the precise shade of meaning of a word.

questions.text: The new policy was hailed as a (i) reform by its supporters, yet its critics saw it as a (ii) measure that left the real problem untouched.
questions.explanation: 'Yet' signals a contrast between the two views. Supporters would praise the policy as a far-reaching reform ('sweeping'), while critics would call it superficial ('cosmetic') because it left the real problem untouched. Option (b) reverses the two words, and supporters would not hail a reform as cosmetic. Option (c) has supporters calling the reform trivial, which is not praise. Option (d) does not fit, because 'hailed' means praised, not unpopular. The answer is (a).

questions.text: Had the team _____ the warning signs earlier, the project would not have collapsed.
questions.explanation: This is a third conditional sentence in inverted form. 'Had the team noticed' is the inverted form of 'If the team had noticed', where 'had' has moved to the front and the past participle 'noticed' follows the subject. Option (c) repeats 'had', which would give 'Had the team had noticed', and that is incorrect. Option (b) is in the present tense, and option (d) uses 'would have' in the condition clause, which is wrong. The answer is (a).

questions.text: Her _____ refusal to compromise, even when the evidence against her position mounted, eventually isolated her from her colleagues.
questions.explanation: The sentence says she refused to compromise even when the evidence was against her, and that this isolated her. The blank needs a word meaning stubborn. 'Obdurate' means stubbornly refusing to change and fits. 'Tentative', 'gracious' and 'flexible' all describe a willingness to yield or a gentle manner, which contradicts a refusal to compromise. The answer is (b).

questions.text: The speaker's remarks, though ostensibly meant to _____ the tension in the room, only served to inflame it.
questions.explanation: 'Ostensibly' means apparently or as claimed, and 'though ... only served to inflame it' signals that the result was the opposite of the stated aim. The stated aim must therefore have been to reduce the tension. 'Defuse' means to reduce tension and fits. 'Aggravate', 'amplify' and 'provoke' all mean to increase tension, which would make the contrast with 'inflame' meaningless. The answer is (c).

questions.text: Hardly _____ the meeting begun when the power went out.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly ... when' is a past-sequence pattern, and when 'hardly' begins the sentence, the auxiliary must come before the subject. Since the later event, 'the power went out', is in the simple past, the earlier event must be in the past perfect, giving 'Hardly had the meeting begun when ...'. 'Has' is present perfect and does not match the past tense. 'Did' would need the base form 'begin', not 'begun'. 'Having' does not make a complete verb phrase here. The answer is (b).

groups.title: Reading Comprehension (Hard): Language Extinction and the Loss of Knowledge

stimulus.text:
Directions: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow on the basis of what is stated or implied in the passage.

Linguists estimate that roughly half of the world's seven thousand languages could disappear within this century. The usual explanation is that small communities abandon their ancestral tongues for dominant languages that offer economic opportunity. This is, in one sense, a rational choice: a parent who encourages a child to learn the language of commerce is hoping to widen that child's prospects. To condemn such parents would be unfair, and any campaign to preserve a language that ignores their reasoning is unlikely to succeed.

Yet the loss is not merely sentimental. A language is not only a means of communication but also a store of accumulated knowledge. Speakers of many small languages possess detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather patterns, built up over generations of close observation. Some of this knowledge has no equivalent in dominant languages, and when the last fluent speaker dies, it may vanish without ever having been written down. Pharmacologists, for example, have occasionally traced useful medicines to plants whose properties were recorded only in the oral traditions of small communities.

Some scholars object that this argument proves too much. If knowledge is what matters, they say, then it is enough to record it, and the language itself can be allowed to fade. A dictionary and a collection of recordings, on this view, are an adequate memorial. Advocates of preservation respond that recorded vocabulary is not the same as living knowledge. A word list cannot capture how a concept is woven into the grammar, the stories and the daily habits of a community; once the people who use the language stop doing so, the records become a museum piece, understood by few and applied by none.

The most promising efforts, therefore, are those that make a language useful rather than merely admired. Programmes that teach it in schools, put it on public signs, and create jobs that require it have had more success than those that only archive it. If a language is to survive, it seems, it must be worth speaking.

questions.text: According to the passage, why do small communities usually abandon their ancestral languages?
options: They are forced to do so by laws passed against small languages.
They hope that learning a dominant language will improve their children's economic prospects.
They no longer find their ancestral languages useful for describing local plants and animals.
Linguists have advised them that the languages cannot survive.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives the usual explanation: communities shift to dominant languages that offer economic opportunity, and a parent who encourages a child to learn the language of commerce is hoping to widen that child's prospects. Option (a) is not mentioned. Option (c) is contradicted, since the passage says these languages hold rich vocabularies for local plants and animals. Option (d) is not stated. The answer is (b).

questions.text: The author mentions pharmacologists in the second paragraph in order to:
options: show that all small languages contain medical knowledge.
give an example of knowledge that has been found in oral traditions and that can be useful beyond the community.
argue that medicine should be taught in small languages.
suggest that the language of commerce is inferior to small languages.
questions.explanation: The example is offered to show that knowledge stored in small languages can have real value, since useful medicines have occasionally been traced to plants described only in oral traditions. Option (a) is an overstatement, because the passage says 'occasionally' and does not say 'all'. Options (c) and (d) bring in ideas that the passage never raises. The answer is (b).

questions.text: The objection of the scholars mentioned in the third paragraph is that:
options: knowledge matters, so recording it is enough and the language itself need not be saved.
a dictionary is not an adequate memorial to a language.
preservation efforts should focus on teaching in schools.
oral traditions have no scientific value.
questions.explanation: The scholars say that if knowledge is what matters, it is enough to record it, and a dictionary and recordings are an adequate memorial, so the language can be allowed to fade. This is option (a). Option (b) is the reply of the advocates of preservation, not the objection. Option (c) comes from the final paragraph. Option (d) is not stated. The answer is (a).

questions.text: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the response of the preservation advocates to the scholars' objection?
options: Word lists and recordings have allowed communities to revive extinct languages, restoring their grammar, stories and daily use.
Many dominant languages also have large dictionaries.
Few linguists are interested in small languages.
questions.explanation: The advocates argue that recorded vocabulary is not the same as living knowledge and that, once people stop using the language, the records become a museum piece. If records have in fact allowed communities to bring a language back into full daily use, this directly weakens the advocates' claim that such records cannot sustain a language's living knowledge. Options (b), (c) and (d) have no bearing on the argument about whether records can substitute for living use. The answer is (a).

questions.text: Which of the following can be inferred from the final paragraph?
options: Archiving a language is more effective than teaching it in schools.
A language is more likely to survive if it gives people practical reasons to use it.
Public signs are the only way to keep a language alive.
Admiration for a language is enough to save it.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says that efforts that make a language useful, by teaching it in schools, using it on signs and creating jobs that require it, have had more success than those that only archive it, and ends by saying that a language must be worth speaking. So a language with practical uses is more likely to survive. Option (a) reverses the finding. Option (c) is an overstatement because signs are only one of several methods. Option (d) is contradicted by the claim that making a language useful works better than merely admiring it. The answer is (b).

stimulus.text: Directions: In each of the following sentences, some part of the sentence or the entire sentence is underlined (shown here in square brackets). Beneath each sentence you will find four ways of phrasing the underlined part. This is a test of correctness and effectiveness of expression. Follow the requirements of standard written English, paying attention to grammar, choice of words and sentence construction. Choose the answer that expresses most effectively what is presented in the original sentence; the answer should be clear and exact, without awkwardness, ambiguity or redundancy.

questions.text: The recent survey shows that the [number of students who prefer online classes are higher than those who prefer classroom teaching].
options: number of students who prefer online classes are higher than those who prefer classroom teaching
number of students who prefer online classes is higher than the number who prefer classroom teaching
number of students preferring online classes are higher than those preferring classroom teaching
number of students who prefer online classes is higher than that of classroom teaching
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the number', which is singular, so the verb must be 'is', not 'are'. The comparison must also be between like things: the number of students who prefer online classes and the number who prefer classroom teaching. Option (b) fixes the verb and keeps the comparison parallel. Option (a) keeps the plural verb 'are'. Option (c) also keeps 'are'. Option (d) compares the number of students with 'that of classroom teaching', which is an illogical comparison. The answer is (b).

questions.text: [Walking along the river bank, a snake was seen by the children] near the old bridge.
options: Walking along the river bank, a snake was seen by the children
Walking along the river bank, the children saw a snake
The children saw a snake, walking along the river bank,
While walked along the river bank, a snake was seen by the children
questions.explanation: The opening phrase 'Walking along the river bank' must modify the subject that follows it. In the original, it appears to modify 'a snake', which is a dangling modifier. Option (b) makes 'the children' the subject right after the phrase, so the modifier is correctly attached. Option (c) places the phrase so that it seems to describe the snake. Option (d) uses the incorrect form 'While walked'. The answer is (b).

questions.text: Rohit, along with his two brothers, [are planning to start a new business, which they hope will be profitable and to provide employment] in the town.
options: are planning to start a new business, which they hope will be profitable and to provide employment
is planning to start a new business, which they hope will be profitable and provide employment
is planning to start a new business, which they hope will be profitable and to provide employment
are planning to start a new business that they hope is profitable and provides employment
questions.explanation: The subject is 'Rohit', and 'along with his two brothers' is only a parenthetical phrase, so the verb must be singular, 'is planning'. The two things hoped for must be parallel: 'will be profitable and provide employment'. Option (b) fixes both problems. Options (a) and (d) use the plural 'are'. Option (c) has the correct verb but breaks parallelism with 'to provide'. The answer is (b).

questions.text: [Unlike the novels of her contemporaries, which focused on the upper classes, Jane's novels] describe the lives of ordinary working people.
options: Unlike the novels of her contemporaries, which focused on the upper classes, Jane's novels
Unlike her contemporaries, which focused on the upper classes, Jane's novels
Unlike the novels of her contemporaries, which focuses on the upper classes, Jane's novels
Unlike her contemporaries' novels, who focused on the upper classes, Jane's novels
questions.explanation: The comparison is between novels and novels, and the original does this correctly: 'the novels of her contemporaries' against 'Jane's novels'. The relative pronoun 'which' correctly refers to the novels, and the plural verb 'focused' agrees. Option (b) compares 'her contemporaries' (people) with novels. Option (c) uses 'focuses', which does not match the past tense and the plural noun. Option (d) uses 'who' for novels, which is wrong. The original is correct, so the answer is (a).

questions.text: The manager insisted that the report [be submitted by Friday and that it includes all the figures for the last quarter].
options: be submitted by Friday and that it includes all the figures for the last quarter
is submitted by Friday and that it include all the figures for the last quarter
be submitted by Friday and that it include all the figures for the last quarter
was submitted by Friday and that it must include all the figures for the last quarter
questions.explanation: After a verb of insistence such as 'insisted that', the subjunctive mood is used, which takes the base form of the verb: 'be submitted' and 'include'. Both parts must use this form to stay parallel. Option (c) does so. Option (a) mixes the subjunctive 'be submitted' with the indicative 'includes'. Option (b) mixes the indicative 'is submitted' with the subjunctive 'include'. Option (d) uses the indicative forms and breaks parallelism. The answer is (c).

standaloneQuestions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?
1) Integer i, j, s
2) Set s = 0
3) For (each i from 1 to 4)
4) For (each j from i to 4)
5) If ((i + j) MOD 2 = 0)
6) s = s + i * j
7) Else
8) s = s - j
9) End-if
10) End-for
11) End-for
12) Print s
standaloneQuestions.explanation: Trace each (i, j) pair with j >= i. i=1: j=1 (sum 2, even) s = 1; j=2 (odd) s = 1 - 2 = -1; j=3 (even) s = -1 + 3 = 2; j=4 (odd) s = 2 - 4 = -2. i=2: j=2 (even) s = -2 + 4 = 2; j=3 (odd) s = 2 - 3 = -1; j=4 (even) s = -1 + 8 = 7. i=3: j=3 (even) s = 7 + 9 = 16; j=4 (odd) s = 16 - 4 = 12. i=4: j=4 (even) s = 12 + 16 = 28. The output is 28.

standaloneQuestions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?
1) Integer func (Integer n)
2) If (n <= 1)
3) return 1
4) End-if
5) If (n MOD 2 = 0)
6) return func(n / 2) + 2
7) Else
8) return func(n - 1) * 2
9) End-if
10) End-function
11) Print func(10)
standaloneQuestions.explanation: func(1) = 1. func(2) = func(1) + 2 = 3. func(4) = func(2) + 2 = 5. func(5) is odd, so func(5) = func(4) * 2 = 10. func(10) is even, so func(10) = func(5) + 2 = 12. The output is 12.

2) For (each i from 1 to 3)
3) t = A[i]
4) A[i] = A[7 - i] + i

6) End-for
7) Print A[1] + A[3] + A[5]

What will be the output of the following pseudocode?
1) Integer n, d, s, c
2) Set n = 2749, s = 0, c = 1
3) While (n > 0)
4) d = n MOD 10
5) If (d MOD 2 = 1)
6) s = s + d * c
7) Else
8) s = s - c
9) End-if
10) c = c + 1
11) n = n / 10 (integer division)
12) End-while
13) Print s + c
standaloneQuestions.explanation: The loop reads digits from the right. d=9 (odd), c=1: s = 9, then c = 2, n = 274. d=4 (even), c=2: s = 9 - 2 = 7, then c = 3, n = 27. d=7 (odd), c=3: s = 7 + 21 = 28, then c = 4, n = 2. d=2 (even), c=4: s = 28 - 4 = 24, then c = 5, n = 0. The loop ends and s + c = 24 + 5 = 29 is printed.

standaloneQuestions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?
1) Integer i, a, b
2) Set a = 3, b = 5
3) For (each i from 1 to 6)
4) If (i MOD 2 = 0)
5) a = a + b
6) Else
7) b = b + a
8) End-if
9) If (a > 20)
10) a = a MOD 7
11) End-if
12) End-for
13) Print a + b
standaloneQuestions.explanation: Start with a = 3, b = 5. i=1 (odd): b = 5 + 3 = 8; a = 3 is not above 20. i=2 (even): a = 3 + 8 = 11; not above 20. i=3 (odd): b = 8 + 11 = 19. i=4 (even): a = 11 + 19 = 30, which is above 20, so a = 30 MOD 7 = 2. i=5 (odd): b = 19 + 2 = 21. i=6 (even): a = 2 + 21 = 23, which is above 20, so a = 23 MOD 7 = 2. a + b = 2 + 21 = 23.

standaloneQuestions.text: A bag contains 4 red, 5 blue and 3 green balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that all three balls are of different colours?
standaloneQuestions.explanation: Total ways to draw 3 balls from 12 = C(12,3) = 220. Favourable ways = 4 × 5 × 3 = 60, one ball of each colour. Probability = 60/220 = 3/11.

standaloneQuestions.text: A boat takes 6 hours to go 24 km upstream and 36 km downstream, and 6.5 hours to go 36 km upstream and 24 km downstream. What is the speed of the stream?
standaloneQuestions.explanation: Let p = 1/(upstream speed) and q = 1/(downstream speed). Then 24p + 36q = 6 and 36p + 24q = 6.5. Multiplying the first by 3 gives 72p + 108q = 18. Multiplying the second by 2 gives 72p + 48q = 13. Subtracting, 60q = 5, so q = 1/12 and the downstream speed is 12 km/h. Then 24p = 6 − 3 = 3, so p = 1/8 and the upstream speed is 8 km/h. Stream speed = (12 − 8)/2 = 2 km/h.

A pacifist is a person who opposes and abstains from war. In the same way, a teetotaler is a person who abstains from alcohol. 'Wine' is too narrow, since a teetotaler avoids all alcohol. 'Thirst' is unrelated. 'Sobriety' is the state a teetotaler enjoys, not the thing they avoid.

standaloneQuestions.text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 20 minutes and pipe B can fill it in 30 minutes, while pipe C can empty the full tank in 15 minutes. Pipe A is opened alone for the first 5 minutes, and then B and C are also opened. In how many minutes in total will the tank be full?
standaloneQuestions.explanation: In the first 5 minutes, A fills 5/20 = 1/4 of the tank. When all three pipes run, the net rate = 1/20 + 1/30 − 1/15 = 3/60 + 2/60 − 4/60 = 1/60 of the tank per minute. The remaining 3/4 of the tank takes (3/4) ÷ (1/60) = 45 minutes. Total time = 5 + 45 = 50 minutes.

standaloneQuestions.text: Two vessels contain mixtures of milk and water in the ratios 3 : 2 and 4 : 1 respectively. In what ratio should the contents of the first and second vessels be mixed so that the new mixture has milk and water in the ratio 11 : 4?
standaloneQuestions.explanation: The milk fractions are 3/5 for the first vessel, 4/5 for the second, and 11/15 for the mixture. By alligation, first : second = (4/5 − 11/15) : (11/15 − 3/5) = (12/15 − 11/15) : (11/15 − 9/15) = 1/15 : 2/15 = 1 : 2. Check: 1 part of the first gives milk 3/5 and 2 parts of the second give milk 8/5, so milk = 11/5 out of 3 parts, which is 11/15.
